newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's new anti-terrorist law under fire.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's new anti-terrorist law under fire.

text.p: Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's new anti-terrorism legislation, designed to curb sectarian violence and terrorism in Pakistan drew scathing criticism from human rights activists and media commentators on Thursday.
The Anti-Terrorism Act, passed by parliament on Wednesday, on the eve of Pakistan's independence anniversary, gives the government sweeping new security powers.
It authorises the security forces to shoot suspected terrorists on sight, search premises and arrest suspects without a warrant, and sets up special fast-track courts to try them.
The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) said it would strike terror into ordinary people, but not deter terrorists.

"The bill is a curious golden jubilee gift which gives sanction to the police to enter and search any house without warrant and even open fire on sheer assumption of terrorist intent," the HRCP said in a statement.
It said terrorism must be curbed, but without giving the police additional coercive powers.
"For all practical purposes, both the investigation and judicial process would end in injustice as is always feared in summary trials," it said.

The bill, an attempt to stop a wave of killings that has shaken Pakistan in the run-up to the anniversary, was passed without amendment thanks to Sharif's large majorities in the National Assembly (lower house) and Senate (upper house).

"Just when this wretched country needed a ray of hope that some day it might revert to the rule of law...this was the last thing it needed," wrote a commentator in the English-language daily The Nation. "Ironically, the new dawn brings suspension of fundamental rights to the extent very rarely accomplished during any civilian rule in the country's history."

The act, which now needs only presidential assent to become law, authorises the federal or provincial governments to call in armed forces to help civilian authorities and prescribes the death penalty for any terrorist whose action has caused a death.

More than 225 people have been killed in a feud involving rival wings of an ethnic party in Karachi so far this year, while a vendetta between militant Sunni and Shi'ite Moslem factions has cost about 140 lives, mostly in Punjab province.
